transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-18 15:00 PST | Duration: ~62m | Recording: yes
Attendees (Redwood): Sofia Park (AE), Daniel Kim (SE), Aria Patel (CSM)
Attendees (Customer): Maya Singh (CTO), Ethan Rivera (SRE), Olivia Chen (PM), Noah Patel (Platform)

Summary: quick sync after yesterday's surge test. Focus: root cause of intermittent 5xxs during burst, validate circuit-breaker approach, decide thresholds for pilot, and run a controlled thundering-herd experiment.

Topics covered: thundering herd symptoms, retry/backoff policy, circuit-breaker design, rate-windowing, host vs dedicated fallback, telemetry gaps, security/compliance ask.

[00:00] Sofia Park: ok hi everyone thanks for carving time; quick roll call then we'll jump into the surge traces Ethan shared.
[00:18] Maya Singh: hi, thanks, yes we saw that spike yesterday around 2pm, lots of concurrent inference calls from checkout flows, basically a hotkey.
[00:26] Ethan Rivera: yeah sorry about the blunt data earlier, i captured some 502/503 spikes and a bunch of client retries that made the tail worse.
[00:34] Daniel Kim: thanks — i pulled the traces from the pilot and the KVcache logs; looks like a combo of request fanout and queue saturation on the shared pool. some of the 5xx correlate with worker OOMs in the dedicated fallback path, maybe due to batch size explosion.
[00:53] Olivia Chen: when you say KVcache, do you mean the prefix caching? we've been seeing cold-starts too when user journeys vary.
[01:01] Daniel Kim: yeah prefix K-V cache, sometimes spelled KV cache in logs — the cold path means more tokens to compute and higher latency leading to timeouts upstream.
[01:12] Noah Patel: quick nuance — we run with hosted for low volume routes and dedicated for high volume, but yesterday the routing went to hosted fallback because dedicated capacity hit its soft limit.
[01:24] Sofia Park: that's a key point; routing policy moved requests and you saw different execution characteristics, so we need to tune routing thresholds and also protect with a circuit breaker before fallback.
[01:35] Maya Singh: can you explain circuit breaker at a high level again? like where it sits and how it trips?
[01:40] Daniel Kim: sure. typical pattern is a token-bucket/rolling-window that monitors error rate and latency; if 5xx rate > threshold or 95p latency > threshold for N seconds, we open the breaker for that route and either (a) serve a cheaper model variant, or (b) fail-fast to the application so it can show cached responses — the goal is to avoid cascading retries.
[02:02] Ethan Rivera: so it prevents the thundering herd from taking down the whole pool by failing fast instead of piling on retries. we had the opposite: clients retried aggressively and made the tail worse.
[02:14] Olivia Chen: on client retries — our frontend has exponential backoff but the jitter is small, so many retries still cluster. we can increase jitter but worried about UX.
[02:26] Sofia Park: common tradeoff. we can also coordinate by setting a retry-budget in the pilot and adding server-side quota hints in the response; Redwood supports a Retry-After header and our SDK honors it.
[02:39] Maya Singh: interesting — does the SDK also stop retries when it sees a circuit-open signal?
[02:44] Daniel Kim: yes, our SDK has a circuit-aware client that respects server signal and will not retry if breaker is open — we'll demo that in the chaos session.
[02:52] Sofia Park: ok let's look at the specific incidents. Daniel, you had 3 representative traces?
[02:56] Daniel Kim: right — i uploaded three short traces to the benchmark sheet. Trace A: a hotkey with 120 concurrent requests within 30s; we saw queue depth spike and latency 95p go to 2.1s with ~1.8% 5xx. Trace B: smaller spike but higher batch-size variance, one worker OOM and 503s followed. Trace C: routing thrash — requests bounced between dedicated and hosted and hit incompatible model variants causing token mismatches and timeouts.
[03:29] Ethan Rivera: that token mismatch bit worried us — are there incompatibilities that cause failures when routing across variants?
[03:35] Daniel Kim: could happen if you're switching quantization profiles or model shims; but we try to ensure model compatibility. in your case, the mismatch was a parameter serialization difference in the custom wrapper — we saw an error that got normalized to a 500 upstream.
[03:49] Olivia Chen: noted — we'll check our wrapper.
[03:52] Maya Singh: what's the recommended immediate defense for the pilot?
[03:55] Sofia Park: short answer: three layers — proactive rate-windowing, server-side circuit-breaker, and client retry-budget + jitter. also adjust batch-size caps on the workers to avoid the batch explosion OOMs.
[04:11] Noah Patel: about batch-size caps — can Redwood enforce max batch size per model route?
[04:16] Daniel Kim: yes, we can set max_batch_size and adaptive batching windowing per route; that prevents runaway batch expansion when many small requests arrive at once.
[04:25] Ethan Rivera: okay, if we cap batch size it may increase p99 a bit but reduce 5xx frequency — acceptable trade.
[04:33] Olivia Chen: on observability — we saw gaps in latency attribution when requests were routed off-cluster; we need clearer traces and example queries to reproduce.
[04:42] Daniel Kim: we'll add tracing hooks and a per-token latency breakdown to the dashboard; i also recommend instrumenting client-side sampling to capture upstream request IDs.
[04:52] Sofia Park: security ask from procurement last week — quick update: SOC2 and KMS docs were sent; any follow-ups?
[04:58] Maya Singh: yes the procurement team wants confirmation that KMS keys can be customer-managed in VPC/private deployment scenario.
[05:05] Aria Patel: short answer: yes, in Redwood Private we support customer KMS/HSM and audit logs; we'll resend the architecture doc.
[05:12] Noah Patel: good. also we need SSO/SAML for our dev team to access console; is that configurable now?
[05:18] Sofia Park: yes SAML SSO and RBAC are available in Dedicated and Private; we will include setup steps in the packet Sofia will send tomorrow.
[05:26] Olivia Chen: back to reliability — do you have suggested circuit-breaker thresholds? we don't want to open too early.
[05:33] Daniel Kim: typical starting point for this workload: open if 5xx rate > 1% over a 30s rolling window OR 95p latency > 1.2s for 60s. but for checkout flows you might want a lower latency threshold. we recommend a conservative canary: open threshold 1.25% 5xx OR 95p>1.5s, with a 30s half-open probe.
[05:58] Maya Singh: can the half-open be controlled per customer route so our big customers get stricter windows?
[06:03] Daniel Kim: yes per-route config, per-model config, and per-traffic-tier. you can set different thresholds per customer segment.
[06:11] Ethan Rivera: timeline and test plan — we propose three steps: (1) apply circuit-breaker config and batch caps to a canary route (~10% traffic), (2) run controlled spike (thundering herd) with 200 concurrent simulated calls, (3) analyze telemetry and tune. can Redwood run step 2 in-host?
[06:27] Daniel Kim: we can run the spike from our load lab against your pilot or provide script you can run in your environment. either works; we prefer in-environment for realism.
[06:36] Sofia Park: schedule chaos injection for the week of 11/30, run the load for 10 minutes per test and ramp gradually.
[06:44] Olivia Chen: agree; can we add failure injection like a few workers returning 502 to see cascading behavior?
[06:49] Daniel Kim: yes we'll coordinate fault injection. we'll also capture request-id mapping so we can trace specific dropped requests.
[06:57] Maya Singh: what about cost impact? if we route to cheaper model variants when breaker opens will that materially reduce token spend?
[07:04] Daniel Kim: yes, fallback to smaller quantized variant reduces per-token cost; it's cheaper and often acceptable for degraded UX during surge. Redwood Optimize can estimate delta once we profile.
[07:14] Noah Patel: curious about reserved capacity — would increasing dedicated pool prevent this entirely?
[07:20] Sofia Park: it would reduce likelihood but can't fully prevent thundering-herd that overwhelms even dedicated pools; plus dedicated costs more. combination of capacity + protective controls is best.
[07:31] Ethan Rivera: for the pilot budget we likely can't double capacity. prefer tuning controls first.
[07:36] Olivia Chen: quick question on telemetry retention — we need 90 days for postmortem; are we able to get that?
[07:42] Aria Patel: retention is flexible; we can offer extended retention as an add-on. i'll include options in the packet.
[07:49] Sofia Park: ok let's capture concrete changes to apply to the canary this week. Daniel?
[07:53] Daniel Kim: list: 1) set circuit-breaker open thresholds to 1.25% 5xx or 95p >1.5s; 2) cap batch_size to 16 for checkout route; 3) enable Retry-After headers and client retry-budget of 3 with jitter; 4) set fallback route to quantized-1b variant on open; 5) add additional tracing for request-id at ingress; 6) throttle routing to dedicated when concurrent requests > configured softlimit.
[08:28] Maya Singh: do we have an idea which of these will be highest impact?
[08:33] Daniel Kim: batch caps + breaker combo will be highest; retry-budget addresses the amplification; fallback reduces cost and stabilizes throughput.
[08:42] Olivia Chen: can we simulate increased jitter on frontend without harming conversion metrics? we'll A/B test on a small cohort.
[08:49] Sofia Park: good plan. we'll also propose a short A/B around fallback UX.
[08:56] Ethan Rivera: one last technical note — the workers that OOM'd flagged GPU memory fragmentation; do you log fragmentation metrics?
[09:03] Daniel Kim: we do expose GPU memory high-water and fragmentation approximations in the runtime metrics; we'll surface them in the dashboard and correlate to batch sizes.
[09:12] Noah Patel: perfect.
[09:15] Olivia Chen: anything on legal/procurement hold-ups?
[09:18] Maya Singh: procurement asked for indemnity language around data residency; we requested clarifications and raised they want it in the contract.
[09:25] Sofia Park: we'll loop in legal; i'll attach the standard clause and the Private deployment option which addresses residency.
[09:31] Daniel Kim: quick note for the checklist for the chaos run: ensure canary headers, set synthetic user IDs to avoid affecting real users, enable full logging for the 10 minute window only.
[09:42] Ethan Rivera: makes sense. we'll prep a staging cluster that mirrors production routing; we'll provide the synthetic traffic profile.
[09:49] Sofia Park: timeline recap: we'll push configs to canary by 11/19, Redwood to share benchmark CSV by 11/20, customer to run initial in-env spike 11/24 and then chaos session with Redwood week of 11/30. does that align?
[10:06] Maya Singh: yes, that's good.
[10:09] Olivia Chen: one more ask — can Redwood include a short runbook excerpt for ops so our on-call knows when to fail open vs throttle?
[10:16] Aria Patel: yes we'll include a 1-page runbook with escalation steps.
[10:20] Sofia Park: great. any final questions?
[10:23] Maya Singh: none from me. thanks for the thoroughness.
[10:27] Sofia Park: thanks all. we'll follow up with the packet and updated benchmark sheet.

Recap / Next steps (verbatim from meeting):
- Redwood will apply conservative circuit-breaker + batch caps to canary route; config to be pushed 2026-11-19.
